Get your kit right and your first track day is a breeze; turn up missing something vital and you can be turned away at scrutineering. This motorcycle track day gear checklist UK riders can actually use runs from the leathers on your back to the tyre pressure gauge in your toolbox, in the order you should buy it. I have kitted out plenty of first-timers, so this is the list I wish someone had handed me before my debut.

Leathers: one-piece versus two-piece

Full leathers are mandatory at virtually every UK track day, so this is the first thing to sort. A one-piece suit offers the best protection and is required for the fast group at many circuits. A two-piece suit that zips together at the waist is accepted for novice and intermediate groups at most organisers and has the bonus of doubling as road kit. For a durable, well-armoured one-piece I rate the RST Pro Series Leathers, while riders wanting the flexibility of a zip-together setup should look at the Alpinestars GP Plus Leather Jacket paired with matching trousers. Whatever you choose, fit is everything: leathers should be snug so the armour stays over your joints.

Back and chest protection

Most suits ship with a basic foam back pad that meets the minimum, but a proper certified back protector is a cheap upgrade that could save your spine. A Forcefield Pro L2 Back Protector offers the higher Level 2 rating and slides straight into the pocket of most suits. Add a Alpinestars Nucleon Chest Protector to guard your sternum and ribs, an area road riders often overlook. Our dedicated guide to motorcycle back protectors explains the CE levels in more detail.

Spend your money from the inside out. A rider in a mid-price suit with a Level 2 back protector and a chest guard is far better protected than one in a flashy suit with the foam pad it came with. Armour does not have to be expensive to save you.

Track gloves and boots

Road gloves rarely have the sliders and reinforcement to survive a track fall, so invest in proper gauntlet-style track gloves that cover the wrist and fasten securely. The Alpinestars SP-8 Gloves are a great value option with hard knuckle protection and palm sliders. For your feet, full-height boots that cover the ankle and shin are required; a pair of TCX RT-Race Boots gives you the ankle protection and toe sliders track riding demands. If you want to compare options, our motorcycle boots guide and knee armour guide are worth a read.

Helmet requirements

Your everyday full-face helmet is fine for a track day provided it is in good condition, meets the current ECE 22.06 standard and has no serious damage or deep scratches to the shell. Some circuits will not accept a helmet older than five years or one that has been dropped, so check the joining instructions. A clear or lightly tinted visor is best for a UK day where the light changes constantly. If you are due an upgrade, our roundup of the best touring helmets UK riders rate has options that work equally well on track.

Paddock kit: tyre warmers and stands

These are not essential for your first novice day but they make life far easier as you progress. Good road tyres warmed up over the first couple of laps are perfectly safe for beginner pace, but a set of Oxford Tyre Warmers gets you grip from the first corner and reduces cold-tyre crashes. To fit them, and to lube your chain and check your tyres between sessions, you will want a paddock stand. An Abba Superbike Paddock Stand holds the bike securely and is a paddock staple.

Tools, tyre pressures and spares

Pack a basic toolkit so you can adjust and fix small things trackside: Allen keys, spanners, a socket set, cable ties, gaffer tape and spare masking tape for your lights. A reliable digital tyre pressure gauge is non-negotiable, because you will want to drop pressures slightly for track use and set them accurately. Useful spares to carry include clutch and brake levers, which are the first casualties of even a gentle tip-over, plus chain lube, a rag and a spare pair of gloves. It is also worth packing a small first aid kit, a torch and a foot pump or compressor so you can reset road pressures before the ride home. A track-prepped sportsbike such as a Suzuki GSX-R1000R or a versatile Kawasaki Ninja 1000SX asks little more than fresh consumables and this modest tool bag.

Your track day gear checklist

  • One-piece or zip-together two-piece leathers that fit snugly
  • CE Level 2 back protector and a chest protector
  • Gauntlet track gloves with knuckle and palm protection
  • Full-height boots covering ankle and shin
  • ECE 22.06 full-face helmet in good condition, clear visor
  • Tyre warmers and a paddock stand (as you progress)
  • Basic toolkit, cable ties, gaffer and masking tape
  • Digital tyre pressure gauge and a foot pump or compressor
  • Spare clutch and brake levers, chain lube and a rag
  • Water, food, sun cream and a folding chair for the paddock

Bringing it together

Buy in the order above and you will spread the cost sensibly while never compromising on the protection that matters. With your kit sorted, read our beginner's guide to motorcycle track days to understand how the day runs, then pick your venue from our rundown of the best track day circuits UK riders love. Get the gear right, arrive prepared and your first day on track will be everything you hoped for.

faq.q: Do I need one-piece or two-piece leathers for a track day?
faq.a: Full leathers are mandatory at virtually every UK track day. A one-piece suit offers the best protection and is required for the fast group at many circuits. A two-piece suit that zips together at the waist is accepted for novice and intermediate groups at most organisers and doubles as road kit. Whatever you choose, fit is everything, so leathers should be snug enough to keep the armour over your joints.

faq.q: How should I prioritise my track day spending?
faq.a: Spend from the inside out. A rider in a mid-price suit with a Level 2 back protector and a chest guard is far better protected than one in a flashy suit with the foam pad it came with. Most suits ship with a basic foam back pad, so upgrading to a certified Level 2 protector and adding a chest protector to guard your sternum and ribs is a cheap, high-value improvement.

faq.q: Can I use my road helmet and gear on track?
faq.a: Your everyday full-face helmet is fine provided it is in good condition, meets the current ECE 22.06 standard and has no serious damage or deep scratches. Some circuits will not accept a helmet older than five years or one that has been dropped, so check the joining instructions. Road gloves and boots, however, rarely have the sliders and reinforcement to survive a track fall, so invest in proper track versions.

faq.q: Do I need tyre warmers for my first track day?
faq.a: Not for a novice day. Good road tyres warmed up over the first couple of laps are perfectly safe at beginner pace. Tyre warmers get you grip from the first corner and reduce cold-tyre crashes as you progress and pick up speed, so they are worth adding later. To fit them and to work on the bike between sessions you will also want a paddock stand.

faq.q: What tools and spares should I pack for a track day?
faq.a: Pack a basic toolkit: Allen keys, spanners, a socket set, cable ties, gaffer tape and masking tape for your lights. A reliable digital tyre pressure gauge is non-negotiable, as you will drop pressures slightly for track use. Carry spare clutch and brake levers, which are the first casualties of a tip-over, plus chain lube, a rag, a small first aid kit and a foot pump or compressor to reset road pressures for the ride home.
